title: A conversation on the mountain
hookLine: a circle of yogis sits down, and Guru Nanak's long dialogue with them begins

cards: The circle is already seated when the poem begins. A gathering of Siddhs, yogis who have given up house and family, settle into their postures and greet the company of holy people around them.
Then a guest speaks, and his first words aren't to them at all. Guru Nanak bows to the One and says he would cut off his own head and set it down before that One, offering body and mind.
Only after that bow does the talking start, and it goes on: question, answer, stanza after stanza.

teach.h: SIDH GOSHT: THE TALK WITH THE SIDDHS.
teach.b: The poem is called the Sidh Gosht. Sidh is the yogi, the one said to have reached the goal; gosht is a discussion, a talk. So: the talk with the Siddhs.
It sits in the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Ramkali, under Guru Nanak's name.

These yogis have come up on this path before, once in a single picture of a lotus and a duck, once in Bhai Gurdas's telling of their meeting on a mountain, and tradition places the conversation up in those heights.
First, this is scripture that keeps the other side's questions. The yogis aren't straw men set up to fall over.

They ask real, sharp things, the kind a serious seeker would ask: who are you, why do you live like that, where did it all begin. The Granth sets their questions down in their own voice, some of them by name.
Second, the manners. The yogis greet the gathering.
In the second stanza, in paraphrase, he asks what use there is in wandering about, since it's truth that makes a person pure, and without the Word no one is set free.
That's a firm view, said plainly, but said sitting down, in a circle, with people who disagree.
Third, the shape teaches. Sikh teaching often comes as song to be sung together.
Here it comes as dialogue, two sides taking turns, so listening is built into the form: a question has to be heard all the way through before it can be answered.

how: The Sidh Gosht is sung in kirtan and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs study it in katha, where a teacher explains the yogis' questions and Guru Nanak's answers one stanza at a time.

o: the talk with the Siddhs, Nanak's dialogue with the yogis
a yogic breathing practice taught on the mountain
a hymn Nanak wrote alone in a mountain cave

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: the yogi said to have reached the goal
the raga the poem sits in

s: the Sidh Gosht keeps the yogis' questions in their own voice
the poem sets down their questions, and some of the yogis by name, before Nanak answers.
the poem opens with Nanak attacking the yogis
it opens with the Siddhs greeting the gathering and Nanak bowing to the True One.

it's built as a conversation: question, answer, question, answer.

games.q: you're a guest in a circle of people who live very differently from you, and you think they're mistaken. what does the poem show Nanak doing first?
o: tell them they're wrong straight away.
bow to the One, then take their questions.
games.why: the opening has him bow to the True One before any argument; then the questions come, and he answers each one.

practice: If you can, play a recording of the first stanzas of the Sidh Gosht; if not, hold the three moves from the hook while the breath slows: the circle sits down, the greeting, the bow.
Then bring to mind one conversation waiting for you, and picture the poem's order: sit down with them, greet them, and bow inwardly to what's true. If you pray, let that bow be to the One.
